text.title: Working Backwards PR/FAQ — Five Phases, Seven Rules
text.summary: Five phases run in order, each able to terminate the review. R1 gates entry, R7 gates exit; the five rules between them keep the document honest enough for R7 to mean anything.

rule.statement: Phase 1 MUST name a customer specifically enough that a real person could be pointed at, and state their problem as something observed on a stated date — a conversation, a support thread, a workaround someone built, a payment someone already makes to a worse option. "Users", "teams", "developers" and "small businesses" are not customers. If two exchanges pass without an articulable customer, the review MUST stop and record `verdict: kill` with `killed_at_phase: 1`.
rule.rationale: Working Backwards (Bryar & Carr, St. Martin's Press, 2021) puts the customer first in the literal ordering of the document, not as a value statement: the announcement cannot be drafted until somebody is named to announce it to. An unnameable customer is the cheapest possible kill — it costs one phase instead of a build.

rule.statement: The press release MUST be written as though the thing already shipped: past or present tense, a dated availability line, and no forward-looking verbs — "will", "plans to", "is going to", "aims to", "roadmap", "coming soon" are forbidden in the headline, subhead and body. It MUST fit one page and MUST contain a headline a customer would repeat, the problem in the customer's own words, what they can now do, and one quote from the named customer of Phase 1.
rule.rationale: Amazon replaced slide decks with written narratives in 2004 — a decision Amazon re-described publicly in its 2018 shareholder letter — precisely because bullets let an author gesture at a benefit without committing to a sentence. Future tense is the same evasion in miniature: "will help teams collaborate" survives scrutiny that "teams now do X instead of Y" does not.

rule.statement: The headline MUST describe what the customer can now do, not what was built. Implementation nouns — the stack, the model, the architecture, the framework, "AI-powered", "platform", "engine" — are forbidden in the headline and subhead. They are permitted in the body only where a customer would care.
rule.rationale: Working forwards means starting from what you can build and searching for someone who wants it. A headline that leads with the implementation is that search, printed. If the customer-facing sentence cannot be written without naming the technology, the concept is a technology looking for a problem.

rule.statement: The customer FAQ MUST contain at least five questions, phrased as the buyer would actually phrase them, and MUST include both (a) what it costs them — money, migration, learning, lock-in — and (b) why not the thing they use today, named. Questions the author enjoys answering do not count toward the five.
rule.rationale: A customer FAQ written as marketing copy answers questions nobody asked and leaves the two that decide the purchase untouched. Cost and the incumbent are the two objections every real buyer raises; a document that dodges them has tested nothing.

rule.statement: The internal FAQ MUST be a separate bank from the customer FAQ, MUST contain at least five questions, and MUST include at least one the author does not want to answer. It MUST list every assumption under `must_be_true` — the statements whose falsity kills the concept — and, for the riskiest one, the cheapest test that would falsify it, stated as an act someone can perform this week.
rule.rationale: Bryar & Carr (2021) describe the internal FAQ as the half that does the work: the customer FAQ sells, the internal FAQ interrogates. Merging them produces a document with no antagonist, and a review with no antagonist returns `proceed` every time.

rule.statement: The record MUST declare `concept_type` and the success measure MUST match it, because the party who can kill the concept differs by type: `commercial` — someone unrelated to you pays the stated price; `internal` — the team whose budget it comes out of would fund it over their own next item; `oss` — a maintainer who is not you is willing to carry it, and the maintenance cost is stated; `nonprofit` — the funder and the beneficiary are different people and both are satisfied; `service` — the hours are billable at the stated rate without you personally delivering them; `creative` — an audience that is not your friends chooses it over free alternatives; `physical` — unit economics survive returns, shipping and a second production run. A success measure that does not name that party is not a measure.
rule.rationale: The five phases are identical across concept types; only the antagonist changes. Naming the antagonist explicitly is what stops an internal platform from being validated against enthusiasm, or an OSS release against stars, neither of which is the thing that fails.

rule.statement: The review MUST end in exactly one of `proceed`, `revise` or `kill`, with a written rationale. It MUST NOT emit a numeric score, rating, weighted total or confidence percentage under any field name. `revise` MUST name the phase to re-enter. `kill` MUST record `killed_at_phase` and is a successful outcome of the review — a run that ends in `kill` counts as the gate working, not as wasted effort. `proceed` is the only state that authorises spec, design or build work, and requires every `must_be_true` to be either confirmed or paired with a falsification test.
rule.rationale: A number can be argued upward by the person who wants the answer; a judgement plus a rationale must be argued against on its merits, and the argument is recoverable later. A gate whose recorded history contains no kills has selected for concepts that survive it, not for concepts worth building — which is why `kill` is contractually a success and not an error state.
